title: Hannah Arendt
keyWorks: The Life of the Mind (1978, posthumous)
summary: Hannah Arendt (1906–1975) was a German-Jewish thinker, a student of Heidegger and Jaspers, who fled Nazism and became an American philosopher. She investigated how totalitarianism arose, what makes human life truly shared, and what it means to think and act in a world inhabited, in her words, by men, not “Man.”
onEmotions: Arendt did not build a theory of feelings and was wary of attempts to build politics on them. What interested her was something else: how feelings are connected with the “world” — the shared space between people. Hence her precise distinctions: loneliness (when you are deserted even by yourself), solitude (when I am in good company with myself) and isolation (when you cannot act together with others). She understood thinking as a silent dialogue with oneself, the “two-in-one.” And against the two burdens of human life — the irreversibility of what has been done and the unpredictability of the future — people, according to Arendt, have two answers: forgiveness and promise. At the root of her hope is “natality”: every human being’s capacity to begin something new.

anxiety.text: Every deed, Arendt wrote, falls into a dense web of other people’s lives, and no one knows where the ripples will go. Anxiety is an honest response to the fact that the future can’t be known for certain. Arendt considered this unknowability not a malfunction but a feature of human life itself: every action sets off a chain of consequences that no one can predict, because we live among many other free people — what she called “plurality.” In The Human Condition she offers not a cure for uncertainty but a way of living with it: the promise. By making promises and keeping their word, people create, in her image, islands of certainty in an ocean of uncertainty. Anxiety can then become not an order to control everything but a hint: where do I need an island to stand on — an agreement with myself or with someone close?
anxiety.practice: Make yourself one small promise for tomorrow that you will definitely keep — say, a walk at lunchtime — and say it aloud. This is your island.

fear.text: In 1933 the Gestapo held the young Hannah Arendt under arrest for eight days, and once released she fled Germany: she knew fear from life, not from books. Your fear is an ancient and honest feeling: it tells you that something important is under threat. Studying totalitarian regimes, Arendt saw how fear and terror separate people: a frightened person is left alone with the threat. Courage for her is not the absence of fear but the readiness to step out of the shelter of private life into the shared world: to speak up, to show yourself to others, to begin something. In this light, fear does not make you weak; it only shows that you are standing on a threshold. And a threshold is easier to cross not alone: a fear spoken to someone stops being isolating.
fear.practice: Tell one person at least one sentence about your fear — aloud, in person or on the phone. Fear that has stepped out into the shared world stops isolating you.

sadness.text: Lessing, Rosa Luxemburg, Benjamin, Jaspers — Arendt gathered them between the covers of one book: people who gave light when everything around was darkening. Sadness needs no justification: it often comes when the world seems to have dimmed. She called this book Men in Dark Times. In the preface she writes that even in the darkest of times we have the right to expect some illumination — and that it comes less from theories and concepts than from the uncertain, flickering and often weak light that some people kindle in their lives and works. There is no need to wait until everything has become clear and the sorrow has gone. It is enough to notice a small light nearby — a person, a book, a conversation, someone’s act — and let it be, without demanding that it dispel all the darkness at once.
sadness.practice: In the evening, step outside or go to a window and find one small light — a lit window, a streetlamp, a candle. Look at it for a minute and remember a person who has brightened your day a little lately.

grief.text: “All sorrows can be borne if you put them into a story” — with these words of Isak Dinesen, Arendt opened the chapter on action in The Human Condition. Your grief is the price of love, and there is nothing in it that needs “fixing.” Arendt wrote that who a person was — their unique “who” — is best preserved not in a list of their qualities but in the story of their life as others tell it. This does not mean the story cancels the pain. It gives it a form and a place in the shared world: the loss stops being only your inner burden and becomes a memory that can be shared with others. By telling about whoever or whatever you have lost, you go on being close to them in your own way.
grief.practice: Tell someone one short story about the person or thing you lost — an episode that shows especially well what they were like. If there’s no one to tell, say it aloud to yourself.

quote.text: All sorrows can be borne if you put them into a story or tell a story about them.
quote.author: Isak Dinesen (Karen Blixen)
quote.source: epigraph to the chapter “Action” in Hannah Arendt’s The Human Condition

loneliness.text: Picture a séance: people sit around a table, and suddenly the table vanishes — nothing connects or separates them anymore. Arendt used this image for the loss of a shared world; loneliness wounds just as deeply, and she understood that as few did. In The Origins of Totalitarianism she distinguishes three states. Isolation — when a person is cut off from common affairs, from the possibility of acting together with others. Solitude — when I am alone but have a companion: myself, with whom I can think and talk. And loneliness — when I am deserted by everyone, even by myself; it can be felt acutely in the middle of a crowd. This distinction gives you something to stand on: loneliness can gradually be turned into solitude by recovering your inner dialogue, and from solitude, for Arendt, it is easier to go out to people again.
loneliness.practice: Go for a short walk and talk with yourself as with a friend: “How are you now?” — and listen to the answer. Arendt would call this solitude: you are not alone while this companion is with you.

quote.text: Loneliness is not solitude. Solitude requires being alone whereas loneliness shows itself most sharply in company with others.
quote.author: Hannah Arendt
quote.source: The Origins of Totalitarianism, “Ideology and Terror”

anger.text: Arendt would ask about your anger not “how do I calm it down?” but “what here could be changed?” Anger is often seen as shameful and “irrational,” but she disagreed. In the essay On Violence she wrote that rage is not necessarily irrational at all: it arises where there is reason to suspect that conditions could be changed and are not, and where our sense of justice is offended. That is, anger can be a sign that you still believe something else is possible. At the same time, Arendt sharply distinguished power from violence: power is born when people act together and come to agreement, while violence only destroys. One conclusion follows: anger deserves to be heard, but its force serves you best when it turns into words and shared action rather than a blow.
anger.practice: Say aloud in one sentence what you think could be different — as if you were speaking at a town meeting. Anger that has become words is, for Arendt, already closer to action than to a blow.

shame.text: For years Arendt worked on a book about a woman who had died long before she was born — and recognized herself in her. Shame makes you want to disappear, to hide what is “wrong” with you. She knew this feeling well from the story of Rahel Varnhagen — the hostess of a Berlin salon at the turn of the 19th century, about whom she wrote a book. For a long time Rahel tried to get rid of her Jewish origins as something shameful, and only at the end of her life accepted them as part of herself. Arendt distinguished the “parvenu,” who is ashamed of himself and tries to look like everyone else, from the “conscious pariah,” who openly acknowledges his difference. Shame, seen this way, weakens when you stop hiding from your own story.
shame.practice: Name to yourself one trait or part of your story you are used to hiding, and say aloud, without apology: “Yes, this is me too.” Arendt would call this the choice of the conscious pariah.

guilt.text: Arendt demanded that we speak of guilt with a judge’s precision: who did exactly what, and when. Guilt can be agonizing, but it has a valuable core: it shows that you care. Guilt, in her view, concerns the specific acts of a specific person; it should not spread over “everything” and turn into a verdict on the whole personality. She even warned that where all are guilty, nobody is — diffuse guilt keeps us from seeing what exactly happened. For you this might mean: try to separate what you actually did from a general feeling of your own “badness.” The first can be thought through, acknowledged, repaired; you can ask for forgiveness. The second is just a heavy fog. Besides, forgiveness for Arendt happens between people: sometimes guilt is eased by a conversation rather than by solitary self-flagellation.
guilt.practice: Choose one part of what you did that can be mended, and take a small step toward it — a message, an apology, repaying a debt. Forgiveness, for Arendt, is born between people.

envy.text: “Who are you?” and “what are you?” are two different questions for Arendt, and for the second there will always be someone with a better answer. Envy does exactly that kind of comparing — he has more, she’s more successful — and it hurts. In The Human Condition she distinguishes the “what” of a person — their qualities, talents, achievements, everything that can be compared with others’ — from “who” they are: the unique person who appears in words and deeds and cannot be ranked alongside others. Envy lives in the world of the “what”: there someone will always be ahead. But what is essential in you is precisely the “who,” and it does not take part in any competition. This does not cancel the wish for more, but it takes the sting out of envy: your place in the world is not taken by others.
envy.practice: Recall one gesture, decision or word of yours that no one else would have repeated — not an achievement, but your own handwriting. Tell someone about it, or simply say it aloud.

emptiness.text: “And what about your world?” Arendt would probably ask not only about you but about that. When everything has lost its color and nothing touches you, emptiness can be very heavy. By “world” she meant not the planet but the shared space between people: the things, affairs, places and conversations that both connect and separate us — the way a table connects and separates those who sit around it. She wrote about the “world alienation” of the modern age, when life is reduced to the cycle of labor and consumption. For Arendt, emptiness may be not a personal defect but a sign that there is less of this “table” between you and the world — fewer shared things and shared affairs. The way back can start small: with one lasting thing, with one task shared with someone.
emptiness.practice: Hold one long-familiar thing — a cup, a book, a key — and remember whom or what it connects you with. It is a piece of the “table” between you and the world.

confusion.text: Socrates, Arendt wrote, was compared to an electric ray: he paralyzed others because he himself was paralyzed by perplexity. Confusion, when familiar supports stop working and it’s unclear what to do, is a hard feeling — but an ancient and honest one. Arendt knew this from her own experience: her era destroyed many traditional answers. She spoke of “thinking without a banister” — the ability to think when you can lean neither on a ready-made theory nor on authority — and considered this perhaps the only honest way to think in a new situation. She described understanding as an unending activity through which we gradually come to terms with reality: it does not hand out final solutions but helps us find our bearings. Confusion, seen this way, is the beginning of understanding, not its failure. You can move without a banister too: slowly, testing each step.
confusion.practice: Go for an aimless walk and hold your question in mind without solving it — just walk with it, as with a companion. Arendt called this thinking without a banister.

fatigue.text: Dishes are washed to be dirtied again, food is cooked to be eaten — Arendt called this “labor” and saw in it an endless cycle. Exhaustion and burnout in such a cycle are not weakness but a response to endlessness. Arendt distinguished three kinds of activity: labor, work and action. Labor serves the cycle of life — food, cleaning, earning a living — and never ends: what is made is immediately consumed, and everything starts again. Modern society, for Arendt, has become a “society of laborers,” in which almost everything has been turned into such a cycle. Her distinction helps you ask: besides endless labor, is there anything in my life that is finished and lasting — something that will remain — or an act that begins something new? Sometimes what drains your strength is not the number of tasks but the fact that none of them brings the feeling of “done.”
fatigue.practice: Do one small thing today that has an end — finish a chapter, sew on a button — and mark the moment of “done” to yourself.

boredom.text: Arendt warned of “a society of laborers without labor”: people freed from work who would not know what to do with their freedom. Boredom seems a trifle, but she would see something telling in it. She wrote that in a society built around labor and consumption, free time easily turns into emptiness, which is filled with new portions of consumption — and the appetite only grows. Boredom then is a signal that the cycle of “make — consume” does not satisfy. Arendt would remind us of other possibilities: thinking, conversation with oneself, action together with others. Thinking for her is not work for the sake of a result but a free activity, valuable in itself. For Arendt, boredom can become an invitation: not to hurry to fill the pause, but to allow yourself to think about something just for its own sake.
boredom.practice: Sit for five minutes without your phone, with one question that’s interesting to think about without an answer — for example: “What did I notice for the first time today?” Let your thought wander just for its own sake.

joy.text: “It is action, not rest, that constitutes our pleasure” — Arendt loved this line of John Adams. If you feel joy right now, let the feeling simply be. Arendt especially valued one kind of joy that is rarely talked about: the joy of acting together. In On Revolution she describes “public happiness” — a special feeling people experience when together they discuss, decide and begin something new, when they are seen and heard. It is not a private pleasure or consumption but the joy of taking part in a shared world. Perhaps your present joy also has something of this — a meeting, a conversation, a task in which you were not alone. And if the joy is quiet and personal, Arendt would remind you that it can be shared, and then it becomes part of the world and not only of your inner space.
joy.practice: Tell someone in a sentence or two what is making you glad right now — just so it sounds out in the world and becomes a little shared.

love.text: “Amo: volo ut sis” — “I love you: I want you to be.” Arendt, who began her path with a dissertation on love, carried this formula of Augustine’s through her whole life, and the tenderness you feel is captured in it very precisely. To love in this sense is not to possess or remake but to want the other to exist as they are. In The Human Condition, Arendt notes something else: love by its nature is “worldless” — it is so focused on one person that everything else seems to vanish. This is not a reproach but a description: love briefly takes us out of the shared world. You can enjoy it, remembering that afterward it usually looks for a way back — into shared affairs, into a home, into the world.
love.practice: Think of someone you love and slowly say to yourself: “I want you to be.” Repeat it three times and notice what changes in the feeling.

gratitude.text: In the thick of the fiercest dispute of her life — over her book on Eichmann — Arendt wrote to Gershom Scholem of her “gratitude for everything that is as it is.” Gratitude is a warm feeling, and she found room for it even in very sober thought. In the prologue to The Human Condition she writes with concern about modern man’s drive to remake the very conditions of his existence — as if life had not been given to him as a free gift from nowhere, secularly speaking. This is not a call to put up with injustice: Arendt argued with injustice all her life. It is a recognition that much — the body, the world, encounters, language — came to us without our ordering it. Gratitude is a way of noticing this givenness.
gratitude.practice: Step outside for five minutes and find three things you neither chose nor “earned” — the sky, the language you think in, someone’s smile. Silently thank each one.

hope.text: “A child has been born unto us” — with these Gospel words, the “glad tidings,” Arendt closes the chapter on action in The Human Condition. Hope rests on the fact that the future is not yet decided, and Arendt gave this an unexpected foundation — “natality.” Every human being, coming into the world, brings into it the possibility of a new beginning, and this capacity to begin stays with us all our lives: in every act, word, decision. That is why human affairs are never fully predictable — something no one expected can always happen. In The Human Condition, Arendt writes that it is precisely the capacity for action that brings into the world faith and hope, which she called the two essential characteristics of human existence. Your hope, seen this way, is not naivety but sober knowledge about the nature of human beings: they know how to begin anew.
hope.practice: Make one very small “beginning” today — call someone, ask something, try something for the first time. Arendt would say this is how hope enters the world.

quote.text: The miracle that saves the world, the realm of human affairs, from its normal, “natural” ruin is ultimately the fact of natality.
quote.author: Hannah Arendt

nostalgia.text: Ariel’s song from Shakespeare’s Tempest — about a drowned man whose bones became coral and whose eyes turned to pearls — was, for Arendt, the finest image of memory. Longing for what was and won’t return in its old form is a poignant feeling. Arendt thought a great deal about the past in an era when, in her words, the thread of tradition had been broken. In her essay on Walter Benjamin she describes a special relationship to the past — like that of a pearl diver, who dives into the depths not to revive what is gone in its entirety but to bring up to the surface individual precious fragments. Nostalgia can be lived the same way: not trying to bring the past back, but carefully retrieving from it what still shines and carrying that into today.
nostalgia.practice: Choose one “pearl” from that time — a habit, a word, a taste, a song — and bring it back into your life today: cook it, play it, say it.

quote.text: Our inheritance was left to us by no testament.
quote.author: René Char
quote.source: quoted by Hannah Arendt in the preface to Between Past and Future

craving.text: Arendt’s last, unfinished book is devoted to three faculties — thinking, willing and judging — and she wrote of the will as a place of inner conflict. A sharp “I want it right now” can be so strong that it seems someone else is deciding for you. Here she drew on Augustine, who described how the will splits in two — one part of it wills, the other does not, and both are me. So a craving is not the whole of you: beside the “I want” another voice is speaking too. Her thought about thinking as a pause helps here as well: to “stop and think” means to interrupt an automatic movement. The wave of craving rises and falls; in that pause you can give the second voice a say, without condemning either of them.
craving.practice: When the craving rises, pause for three breaths — Arendt called this “stop and think.” On the first out-breath name the voice that says “I want,” on the second the voice that says “I don’t,” and on the third simply wait for the wave to subside.

addiction.text: A circle with no beginning and no end, where one satisfaction immediately demands the next — this is how Arendt described a life ruled by necessity alone. Getting out of the old circle of addiction is hard, and not at all because a person is “weak.” But perhaps the most important thing she can offer here is her thought about forgiveness and promise. Both of these capacities, she wrote, depend on the presence of other people: no one can forgive himself, and no one can really be bound by a promise made only to himself. Many attempts to get out alone are hard not for lack of will but because a promise needs a witness. Hence the value of places where people keep their word together and don’t turn away from one another after a relapse.
addiction.practice: Name to yourself one person or place — someone close, a mutual-help group — that could witness your small promise. Decide nothing; simply note that such a witness exists.

hangover.text: What’s done can’t be undone — Arendt called this “irreversibility” and saw it as the common lot of everyone who acts, not as anyone’s special vice. On the morning after, when your body aches and anxiety, shame and blanks are spinning in your head — what did I say, what did I do? — this thought rings especially sharp. Her answer to irreversibility is forgiveness — but forgiveness, for Arendt, happens between people: you cannot issue it to yourself. That is why endless self-flagellation in the morning fixes nothing. It is more honest to calmly find out what really happened and, if necessary, talk to whoever it concerns. And in the meantime, take care of yourself and pass no verdicts: you are still someone capable of beginning anew.
hangover.practice: Sit by a window and calmly name aloud only what you know for sure about last night. Set the rest aside until you can talk with whoever it concerns: forgiveness, for Arendt, happens between people.

euphoria.text: “The miracle that saves the world from ruin is natality,” Arendt wrote: again and again, something new enters the world. Right now, when everything seems possible and the world flung open, she would not spoil this burst. The capacity to begin, which she called “natality,” makes the unexpected possible. But she also noted that action is by nature boundless: what has been begun goes out into the world and produces consequences that can be neither predicted nor taken back. That is why people have long set limits to action — laws, promises, boundaries. Euphoria can be lived in this spirit: rejoicing in the feeling of openness, but not rushing to turn every idea into an irreversible step. Let the high be a beginning, and let decisions wait until they can be discussed more calmly — with yourself and with someone you trust.
euphoria.practice: Write down the ideas being born into a list of “beginnings” and set it aside for a couple of days: let decisions wait for a calm conversation with yourself and with someone you trust.

crash.text: “Is this a defeat — or just a rhythm?” Arendt would probably ask. The drop after a high — a celebration, a success, excitement — can be especially bitter: as if you’d been thrown from a height. She wrote that the life of the body moves in a cycle — exertion and exhaustion, rise and fall; that is how the very “labor” of life is arranged. The fall is part of the cycle, not a verdict on what was at the top. She also spoke of the “frailty of human affairs”: everything that arises between people — a celebration, a shared impulse, a success — cannot last forever on its own. What helps preserve it is not new highs but memory and storytelling. You can treat the comedown like an ebb tide: it doesn’t cancel the flood tide and says nothing about your worth.
crash.practice: Recall three good moments from the high and retell them to yourself aloud as a short story — so that memory keeps more than “and then it got bad.”

panic.text: Arendt didn’t write about panic, but she has a simple image — a table that stays in place while we change — and here it unexpectedly helps. Panic is terrifying: a wave of dread, your heart, your breath, the sense that something irreversible is about to happen. Such a wave usually peaks and recedes within a few minutes. In The Human Condition Arendt notes that the things of the world — a table, a chair, walls — stabilize human life: we constantly change, but by returning to the same table and the same chair we find ourselves again. The world is more durable than our states. When there is a storm inside, you can lean on this durability: the things around you stay in their places; they hold you. You don’t need to defeat the panic — it is enough to hold on to the world while the wave passes.
panic.practice: Place both palms on a table or wall and press — feel that the world is staying put. Breathe out longer than you breathe in, and name aloud the things you touch or see until the wave begins to ebb.

dread.text: As a student in Marburg, Arendt listened to Heidegger, for whom the human being is above all “being-toward-death.” Dread before the question “why any of this, if everything ends” is one of the heaviest experiences, and there is nothing shameful in it. But Arendt deliberately shifted the emphasis. She wrote that human beings, though they must die, are not born in order to die but in order to begin. What became central for her was not mortality but “natality” — the capacity to bring something new into the world. This shift does not cancel finitude, but it changes the direction of your gaze: meaning doesn’t have to be derived from the abyss; it is created by beginnings, deeds, connections with others. The answer to such a question is not built alone or in a single night.
dread.practice: Recall one “beginning” in your life that changed something — a meeting, a decision, a first step — and imagine a world in which it never happened. What came into being because of it?

fomo.text: “Would you want to be there if no one saw it?” — that’s the question Arendt might ask. When it feels like life is happening somewhere else, where the others are, it’s unsettling and it stings. Arendt would explain much of this through the difference between “the social” and a genuinely shared world. “Society” in her language is a space where everyone behaves alike, compares themselves with the norm and is afraid of falling behind. A genuinely shared world is a “space of appearance,” where a person shows themselves to others as a unique “who” through their words and deeds. In this light, you are missing nothing where all that is required is conformity. What matters more is this: where can you yourself appear — say something, do something, begin something with the people around you?
fomo.practice: Do something today together with a person near you — not for the feed and without photos: a talk, a walk, a shared task. This is the “space of appearance” Arendt spoke of.

sleepless.text: Penelope unraveled at night what she had woven by day — Arendt saw in this a precise image of thinking. Sleeplessness with three-in-the-morning thoughts is exhausting: the mind spins and there are no answers. Arendt thought a great deal about what thinking is, and her observation is comforting here. Thinking, she wrote in The Life of the Mind, does not produce results the way a craft does. That is, night thoughts don’t have to arrive at a decision — and when they don’t, it isn’t your fault. Besides, thinking for her is a dialogue with oneself, the “two-in-one.” At night this dialogue often turns into an interrogation. You can gently give it back a friendly tone: I don’t have to solve everything now; we’ll talk about this in the morning, in daylight and among other people.
sleepless.practice: Rest your palm on your belly and on each out-breath silently tell the spinning thought: “In the morning, in the light.” The nighttime dialogue with yourself doesn’t have to be an interrogation.

betrayal.text: “Islands of predictability in an ocean of uncertainty” — that is what Arendt called the promises on which life together rests. Betrayal wounds especially deeply because such an island gives way beneath your feet. In her understanding, the promise is the chief way people create a little reliability in an unpredictable world. A broken promise is not a trifle but a blow to the very foundation of life together, and your pain is proportionate to that. Arendt also spoke of forgiveness — as the capacity to release both yourself and the other from an endless chain of consequences. But forgiveness for her is a free act, a new beginning, not a debt that can be demanded. You can first simply acknowledge the scale of what was broken and give yourself time. Forgiveness, if it comes, will be your own beginning, not someone else’s demand.
betrayal.practice: Say aloud one precise sentence: exactly which promise — spoken or unspoken — was broken. Precision is the first form of respect for your own wound.

jealousy.text: In Augustine’s formula of love that Arendt cites — “I love you: I want you to be” — there is no word “mine.” When a mixture of love, fear of loss and pain torments you, that difference is easy to forget. Jealousy, though, often asks for guarantees and possession, while Arendt insisted that another person always remains a unique “who” who cannot be appropriated or fully predicted. This unpredictability is frightening, but it is also what keeps love alive. People respond to it not with control but with promises — free and mutual. You can listen to jealousy as a question: what would I like to come to an agreement about with the person I love?
jealousy.practice: Ask yourself what you’re afraid of losing, then think about what mutual promise you could calmly talk over with this person. Choose a quiet moment for that conversation.

resentment.text: Arendt named Jesus of Nazareth as the discoverer of the role of forgiveness in human affairs — and spoke of forgiveness in entirely secular terms. Old resentment is like a load you carry for years. Arendt explained why this happens: what has been done is irreversible, and without some kind of release we remain chained to a single deed — our own or someone else’s. Forgiveness, in her words, is the only reaction that does not merely re-act to an injury, repeating it, but begins something new and unexpected, freeing both the one who forgives and the one who is forgiven. Importantly, Arendt saw forgiveness as a free act, not an obligation. You may not forgive for now — and still notice that the grievance keeps you in the past, and ask yourself whether you would like to be free someday. That question alone already loosens the chain a little.
resentment.practice: Walk for a few minutes and on the way ask yourself, as you would a companion: “Do I ever want to be free of this resentment?” You don’t have to forgive — an honest answer is enough.

quote.text: The possible redemption from the predicament of irreversibility — of being unable to undo what one has done though one did not, and could not, have known what he was doing — is the faculty of forgiving.
quote.author: Hannah Arendt

heartbreak.text: As a young student, Arendt went through an agonizing love affair with her professor and left Marburg for Heidelberg to start over. A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains, and there’s no need to rush it. Arendt observed that love, while it lasts, is “worldless”: it gathers the whole world into one person, and between two lovers everything else disappears. That is why after a breakup it feels as if the whole world has collapsed — it really was concentrated in a single point. Her thought suggests a way back: the world is still there — shared affairs, friends, places, things — and gradually it becomes visible again. Arendt also believed in the power of storytelling: the story of a relationship, told to someone, over time turns from an open wound into a part of your life. Not right away — but it happens.
heartbreak.practice: Go today to one place in the “wider world” you haven’t noticed in a long time — a park, a library, a street — and simply be there among people for five minutes.

impostor.text: Who knows better who you are — you, or the people who see your work? Arendt gave an unexpected answer, and it matters when you feel you’re about to be found out. In The Human Condition she writes that “who” a person is shows itself in their words and deeds and is clearly visible to others, yet hidden from the person themselves — like the daimon of Greek belief, which accompanies a person over their shoulder and is visible to everyone except them. So your own judgment of yourself is not the most reliable source. People who value you see what is hard to make out from the inside. Self-doubt is natural, but it doesn’t prove you are a fraud: perhaps others simply see your “daimon” better than you do.
impostor.practice: Ask someone who knows your work well what they think you do well — and hear it out without interrupting or arguing. It is a view of your “daimon” from outside.

self_hatred.text: “It is better to be at odds with the whole world than, being one, to be at odds with myself” — Arendt returned again and again to these words of Socrates. When the inner critic won’t be quiet, it is real pain, and she gave us a language to speak of it. Thinking, in her view, is a silent dialogue, the “two-in-one”: I talk with myself. Drawing on Socrates, she held that the main condition for living with yourself is to be at peace with this inner partner, to be its friend: after all, you can never get away from yourself. The inner critic is a partner who has turned into a prosecutor. You can disagree with it and gradually give your inner partner back the role of a friend — someone who asks questions rather than passes sentence.
self_hatred.practice: Go for a short walk and let your inner critic say one sentence. Then answer it, aloud or in a whisper, the way a kind friend would — let the companion become a friend again.

helplessness.text: Strength, for Arendt, belongs to an individual, while power arises only between people when they act together — and vanishes the moment they disperse. When it feels like nothing depends on you, it’s exhausting. That is why a person left alone almost always feels powerless — and this is not a personal shortcoming but a feature of the situation she called isolation. An isolated person cannot act, but that does not mean action is impossible altogether. For Arendt, powerlessness says not “I am worthless” but “I am alone with this.” Even a small joining together — a conversation, a shared request, a joint step — changes the balance: where two people have come to an agreement, a little power appears.
helplessness.practice: Call or go up to one person and ask them to share a small part of what feels unbearable. Where two people have agreed, for Arendt, there is already a little power.

procrastination.text: A first line, a first call, a first step — Arendt considered every beginning a small miracle, and miracles don’t happen on schedule. When “I can’t start” drags on for days, it’s agonizing. Arendt considered the capacity to begin the deepest feature of the human being and often recalled Augustine’s words: “That a beginning be made, man was created.” But she also understood why beginning is hard: a beginning is a step into the unknown, its consequences cannot be predicted, and it is easy to freeze on the threshold. In this light, procrastination is not laziness but a collision with the weight of beginning. It helps to shrink its scale: a beginning doesn’t have to be grand. Any small action — the first line, the first phone call — already brings something new into the world, and after that the task gradually begins to sustain itself.
procrastination.practice: Make the smallest possible beginning — one line, one call, five minutes — and stop, without thinking about what comes next.

uprooted.text: For eighteen years Hannah Arendt lived without citizenship, a person no state recognized. She knew uprootedness from the inside: in 1933 she fled Germany, lived for years as a refugee in France, then made her way to the United States. In the essay “We Refugees” she described this loss: the home is lost, and with it the familiarity of daily life; the occupation is lost; the language is lost, in which reactions were natural. With bitter irony she also wrote about refugees’ attempts to become “like everyone else” as quickly as possible. But many years later, asked what remained of her former life, she said: the mother tongue remains. Some roots travel with us — language, memory, friendships, a way of thinking. The loss is real, and it can be mourned; but you have not been left entirely without ground.
uprooted.practice: Say aloud in your mother tongue one phrase, song or saying you have “carried” with you. Arendt would say: this root is always with you.

overload.text: “What are we doing when we think?” Arendt asked this all her life, and the beginning of the answer is simple: we stop. Overload from the endless feed and information noise is exhausting, and it’s not about your weakness. Arendt believed that thinking requires a special step — a withdrawal from the world of appearances, from the continuous flow of impressions. She called it “stop and think.” Thinking, in her words, is always somewhat “out of order”: it interrupts ordinary activities. When the flow is never interrupted, there is no room left for the inner dialogue, and we merely react. Arendt also distinguished one’s own judgment, formed in conversation with oneself and with others, from a collection of other people’s ready-made opinions. Overload is a signal that the mind needs a pause — not as a luxury but as a condition for being yourself again.
overload.practice: Close the feed, put your phone face down, and sit in silence for three minutes with one question: “What of all I’ve seen today do I actually want to think over?”

unreality.text: How do we know the world is real at all? Arendt answered unexpectedly — through other people; and the feeling that nothing is quite real is frightening and disorienting, and deserves to be spoken of gently. In The Human Condition she writes that the reality of the world and of ourselves is assured by the presence of others — by the fact that others see what we see and hear what we hear. The shared sense of reality — “common sense” in the old meaning of the word — takes shape between people, and in loneliness, she noted, it can weaken. In this light, a feeling of unreality doesn’t necessarily mean something is “wrong” with you; sometimes what helps is a simple return to the shared world — a voice, a glance, a task done together.
unreality.practice: Describe aloud to someone — or in a voice message — what you see around you right now, and ask them what they see. Notice how the world “meets” between you.

awe.text: The first step of philosophy, for Arendt, was not doubt but speechless wonder that anything exists at all — following Plato, she called it thaumazein. The awe you feel before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious feeling of the same kind. In The Life of the Mind she describes it as admiring wonder, out of which thinking grows. She also greatly valued the durability of the world: works of art, in her view, are the most “worldly” of things; they outlast generations and allow mortal people to encounter something permanent. Perhaps your awe is just such an encounter with something greater and more lasting than you. It doesn’t need explaining; it is enough to let it last and perhaps become the beginning of a thought.
awe.practice: Stay in this feeling a minute longer, saying nothing and taking no photos. Then let one question be born from it — and simply hold it in mind.

relief.text: The chain of consequences that trails every deed does sometimes break — and Arendt saw real liberation in such moments. Relief feels as if whatever held you has let go. Arendt described something similar when she spoke of forgiveness: it releases us from the consequences of what was done and allows us to begin anew. In general, her philosophy is largely about such releases: irreversibility and unpredictability are hard conditions of human life, but people have ways of living with them. Relief may be a sign that one of these releases has happened: an uncertainty has been resolved, someone has kept their word, you have forgiven or been forgiven. There is no need to immediately look for the next worry to fill the space that has opened up. Let yourself simply stay in the moment when the chain of anxiety has broken and you can go on living.
relief.practice: On a slow out-breath, name exactly what has let you go, and say aloud: “It’s over.” Listen to how the words sound.

calm.text: Thinking, for Arendt, is the one activity that requires nothing but yourself. Calm and peace are a time when you can be with yourself without hurry. Arendt valued this state highly and called it solitude. Unlike loneliness, in solitude a person is not deserted: they are in the good company of themselves, and a quiet conversation goes on between them and themselves. It is here, for Arendt, that thinking is born. She ends The Human Condition with Cato’s words, as reported by Cicero: never is a man more active than when he does nothing, never is he less alone than when he is by himself. Your calm, seen this way, is neither emptiness nor idleness but a special kind of activity: being present with yourself.
calm.practice: Sit in silence for a few minutes and ask yourself, as a friend: “What would you like to think about?” You don’t have to answer — it’s enough to be in good company.

inspiration.text: A carpenter sees the future table in advance, while someone acting among people doesn’t know where their deed will lead — Arendt distinguished these two ways of bringing something new. Inspiration is the joyful sense that something new is being born inside you. Arendt would see in it an expression of that very capacity to begin which she placed at the center of human life — “natality.” She also has a distinction that helps you understand where inspiration can lead. Work (fabrication) is the making of durable things: books, paintings, houses that remain in the world after us. Action is deeds and words among people that reveal “who” you are. Its value is that it brings into the world something that was not there before. You don’t need to know in advance how it will all end: a beginning, for Arendt, is never predictable anyway.
inspiration.practice: Turn the idea into a first step you can take today: a sketch, a call, a conversation. You don’t need to know how it ends — a beginning, for Arendt, is never predictable anyway.

schadenfreude.text: Kant, whom Arendt read all her life, suggested testing a judgment with a simple question: could you say it aloud in front of everyone? Almost everyone has felt secret pleasure at someone else’s failure, though people rarely speak of it. Arendt, drawing on Kant, thought a great deal about judgment — about how we assess what we see. She noticed an important criterion: genuine judgment is “communicable”; it can be voiced before others and can ask for their agreement. This requires an “enlarged mentality” — the ability to put yourself in other people’s places in thought. Arendt would probably say that schadenfreude is a pleasure that does not stand up well to this test: it is hard to share openly, especially with the person who failed. But it hints that for now you are looking only from your own place.
schadenfreude.practice: In your mind, “go visiting” the person who failed — following Kant, Arendt called this enlarged thinking. Look at what happened through their eyes for a minute and notice what is left of the gloating.

contempt.text: The question “who is this person?” can’t be answered with a list of qualities — a great deal in Arendt rests on this idea. Contempt, though, arises when someone seems unworthy, stupid or pitiful. She distinguished between the “what” and the “who” of a person. The “what” is a set of qualities: profession, mistakes, flaws, social role. The “who” is the unique person who is revealed in words and deeds and can never be reduced to a list of properties. Contempt, seen this way, sees only the “what” — and confuses an act with the whole person. Arendt did not, however, call on us to give up judgment: she insisted that acts must be judged, and she herself judged harshly. This distinction helps: you can clearly reject what someone has done without turning them into something worthy only of contempt.
contempt.practice: Look at this person (or picture them) and find one thing that speaks of their “who” rather than their “what” — a gesture, a tone of voice, care for someone. You can still reject what they did.

disgust.text: “Yuck” is not yet a judgment, but a judgment can begin with it — that’s roughly how Arendt might put it. Disgust is an instant, almost bodily reaction, and it comes on its own. In her lectures on Kant’s political philosophy, Arendt drew attention to something unexpected: Kant modeled the faculty of judgment on taste — the most personal of the senses, which immediately says “it pleases me” or “it doesn’t.” But judgment differs from mere taste in that reflection takes part in it: we step back, imagine other people’s points of view and ask whether they would share our reaction. For Arendt, disgust is raw material, a first “I don’t like this,” and it is legitimate. But it can be turned into judgment if you ask: what exactly repels me, and how would someone else see it?
disgust.practice: Imagine how a calm, well-meaning observer would describe the same scene, and say that description aloud in one sentence. Notice whether the disgust holds or softens.

revenge.text: Revenge is as predictable as an echo, while forgiveness is always unexpected — Arendt builds a whole philosophy of action on this distinction. The wish for revenge is a very human answer to harm done to you. She called vengeance the natural, automatic reaction to a trespass — predictable, almost inevitable. The problem with revenge, for Arendt, is that it continues the chain: every response provokes a new response, and the participants end up bound to the original deed. She considered the opposite of vengeance to be forgiveness — the only action that does not merely react but begins something new, freeing the one who forgives as well. Arendt did not demand that everything be forgiven: she believed some deeds are unforgivable, and she granted punishment its place. But from her point of view it is important to see that revenge keeps you in the past.
revenge.practice: Imagine two continuations of this story: in one you answer with revenge, in the other with protection, refusal or a just demand. Live through each in your mind for a minute and notice which leaves you freer.

anger_at_loved.text: Arendt defined respect as “a kind of friendship without intimacy” — a distance that lets you see the other as a separate person. Anger at those closest to you — a partner, parents, children — may arise precisely because there is almost no such distance with them. Arendt wrote that between people there needs to be a “world” — a shared space that both connects and separates them, like a table people sit around. Love, as she observed, destroys this in-between: in closeness no gap remains. That is why clashes in close relationships are so sharp — there is no space where the tension could dissipate. It follows that anger at loved ones does not cancel love but speaks of a lack of this “in-between.” Sometimes restoring a little space — stepping out, keeping quiet, talking later — means protecting both yourself and the relationship.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger rises, say “I need five minutes,” go into another room and simply stand by the window for five slow breaths. This is your “table” between you — afterward it will be easier to talk.

ambivalence.text: “Two-in-one” — that is how Arendt described thinking: inside each of us there is a companion with whom we argue, agree and doubt. To love someone and at the same time be unable to stand them is an inner dispute that is hard to bear. She considered this inner dialogue not a weakness but a condition of thinking and conscience. In other words, mixed feelings are also an inner conversation in which several voices are heard. There is no need to force one of them to be silent. Arendt also distinguished between the “what” and the “who” of a person: you may be unable to stand some of the “what” — traits, habits, deeds — and still love the “who,” the unique person. Mixed feelings are a sign that you see a person not in a simplified way but in all their complexity.
ambivalence.practice: Walk for five minutes and let both voices speak in turn: one sentence from “the one who loves,” one from “the one who finds it hard.” Don’t pick a winner.

guilty_relief.text: Feeding, cleaning, caring — Arendt called all this work of sustaining life “labor.” Relief after a breakup, a departure or the death of a gravely ill loved one is often accompanied by shame. This labor never ends and leaves no visible result; it consumes strength the way biological necessity itself does. Caring for someone who is ill, or living through a drawn-out hard situation, is exactly this kind of labor, sometimes for years. Arendt would probably say that relief is a natural response to an endless cycle finally being broken. It does not cancel love: love and exhaustion existed side by side all that time. Arendt also spoke of the inner dialogue with oneself. In it you can honestly admit both feelings without choosing between them.
guilty_relief.practice: Say two sentences to yourself in a low voice, one after the other: “I am so tired of…” and “I loved and I love…” — and listen to how they sound together, without choosing between them.

indifference.text: “What do I think is right to do here?” Arendt would probably put this question above the question of feelings. Sometimes, where something “should” move you, it is quiet inside, and anxiety joins in: is this callousness? Arendt was skeptical of the demand for the “right” feelings. In On Revolution she showed how the demand for visible compassion and sincerity of feeling can turn into suspicion and a hunt for “hypocrites.” What mattered more to her was not what a person feels but how they think, judge and act. Solidarity, for Arendt, is a principle that guides actions, not an emotion you have to summon up in yourself. Carrying Arendt’s thought further, the absence of strong feeling does not make you a bad person. You can honestly admit, “Right now I don’t feel much,” and still think, judge and act as you believe is right.
indifference.practice: Do one small thing you consider right in this situation — call, help, show up — without waiting for the “proper” feeling to arrive.

escape.text: Freedom of movement — the chance to leave and begin anew — Arendt, in her speech on Lessing, called historically the oldest and most elementary of freedoms. The wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — is known to anyone tired of monotony. She herself was more than once forced to leave and start over in another country and another language. Her central concept is “natality”: every person’s capacity to begin something new, because each of us is born as a new beginning. For Arendt, the wish to escape is the voice of this capacity to begin. It doesn’t necessarily mean you need to leave. Sometimes something new can be begun in the same place. But the impulse itself speaks of something important: you are not reducible to the role you have ended up in.
escape.practice: Imagine beginning something new without going anywhere: a new route, a new task, a new conversation. Choose one such idea and try it on in your mind for tomorrow.

forbidden_attraction.text: At twenty-two, Arendt defended a dissertation on love in Augustine — on love as desire, always reaching for a good we don’t have. Attraction to someone unavailable or “wrong” can be strong and tormenting. She examined his idea of love as desire (Latin appetitus) — a striving toward a good we do not have. Such desire, as she read Augustine, is always accompanied by fear: we are afraid of not attaining what we desire, or of losing it. Arendt showed that desire is defined by its object — it pulls us out of ourselves toward what appears to be a good. Arendt suggests that forbidden attraction tells you what good seems necessary to you right now. It is neither a verdict nor a command. You can look at the desire itself with curiosity: what is it really calling you toward, and what good is missing from your life?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Take a five-minute walk and on the way ask yourself: “What good do I see in this attraction — attention, aliveness, understanding, freedom?” Name one word.

social_anxiety.text: Courage, for Arendt, isn’t only for heroes: it’s needed the moment a person leaves home and begins to speak in front of others. Fear of people and their judgment can freeze you, and that is hard. She also spoke of the “space of appearance”: there, among people, “who” you are is disclosed. And here is what matters: this “who” is more visible to others than to yourself. Arendt compared it to the Greek image of the “daimon” that sits over a person’s shoulder and is visible to everyone but them. It follows that it is impossible to fully control the impression you make on others — and unnecessary. This is freeing: your task is not to look flawless but to appear and speak. The rest, as Arendt believed, is the shared business of everyone who sees you.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, repeat to yourself: “I don’t need to control how I’ll be seen. It’s enough to show up and say one thought of my own.”

uncertainty.text: Arendt has no recipe for making the future known — but she has a way of living when it isn’t. Uncertainty is unsettling: you don’t know what will happen and can’t prepare. Arendt considered unpredictability an ineradicable part of human life. Every action sets off a chain of consequences that cannot be fully foreseen, because we live among other free people, and each of them acts too. She wrote that the remedy for unpredictability is the capacity to make and keep promises. A promise doesn’t make the future known, but it creates “islands of certainty” within it. In other words, uncertainty doesn’t mean there is nothing to lean on. You can lean on what you yourself can promise to yourself and others — however small. These islands won’t cancel the unknown, but they will give you solid ground under your feet.
uncertainty.practice: Arrange a small meeting or call with someone this week — a shared island of certainty the two of you build together.

quote.text: The remedy for unpredictability, for the chaotic uncertainty of the future, is contained in the faculty to make and keep promises.
quote.author: Hannah Arendt

waiting.text: Between Past and Future — Arendt gave that title to one of her collections, and it is an exact name for any waiting. When you’re waiting for an answer, results, news, it’s as if you’re hanging in that gap. In the preface she examines Kafka’s parable of a man pressed by the past from one side and by the future from the other, standing in the gap between them. Arendt believed that it is precisely in this gap, in the present, that thinking lives. Arendt would probably say that waiting is agonizing when we want to leap over the gap as quickly as possible. But this in-between time is not emptiness: in it you can think, reflect, prepare. She showed that the present, even an anxious one, is the place where a person is able to think and remain themselves.
waiting.practice: While you wait, walk for five minutes and ask yourself: “What can I understand now, in this gap, that I wouldn’t have understood without the waiting?”

regret.text: The meaning of a deed, Arendt wrote, is revealed not to the one who acts but to the storyteller — and often only much later. Regret over what you did or didn’t do can come back again and again. She wrote about the “irreversibility” of action: what has been done cannot be undone, even if we did not and could not know what it would lead to. This is one of the hardest conditions of human life. But Arendt also pointed to the way out that human beings have — forgiveness. We can forgive others and accept forgiveness — and this frees us from the burden of the past, giving us the chance to begin again. Carrying Arendt’s thought further, regret does not have to become a lifelong sentence. The past is irreversible, but the capacity to begin something new, according to Arendt, is given to every human being at birth.
regret.practice: Tell yourself this story aloud the way you would tell it about someone close to you — understanding what they didn’t know at the time.

longing.text: Arendt did friendship as seriously as she did thinking: her correspondence with Jaspers and Mary McCarthy stretched over decades. Missing a particular person is pain for someone irreplaceable. She insisted that every person is unique: the world is inhabited by people, not by “Man” in general. In her essay on Lessing she wrote that friendship creates a special shared world between people, which exists only as long as they are together. For Arendt, you long not only for the person but also for this shared world — the conversations, jokes and glances that were possible only with them. That is why no one else can fill this place. Arendt believed that memory and storytelling preserve such a world. By telling about the person, you hold on to what was between you. Longing is an acknowledgment that this person opened up a world for you that no one else did.
longing.practice: Tell someone one story or joke that existed only between you and this person. That is how a shared world goes on living in the telling.

world_pain.text: In 1940 Arendt was held in the Gurs internment camp; before that she had fled the Nazis and lived for years without citizenship — she knew dark times from the inside. Pain for the world — from wars, injustice, hard news — can feel unbearable. Her book Men in Dark Times is about those who kept their humanity when all around was bleak. Arendt valued the effort to understand: not to forgive or justify, but to understand how such things are possible — so as not to be left with horror alone. She also distinguished pity, which can be devastating, from solidarity — a principle that unites people for a common cause. Arendt suggests that you don’t have to contain all the pain of the world, but you can keep your own small light — understanding, a deed, a connection with people.
world_pain.practice: Choose one cause in which you can show solidarity this week — helping a neighbor, supporting a shared effort, showing up where people are needed — and take the first small step.

quote.text: Even in the darkest of times we have the right to expect some illumination.
quote.author: Hannah Arendt

rejection.text: After her book on Eichmann, many old friends turned away from Arendt, but she would not win them back by renouncing her own thoughts. Rejection hurts: you weren’t accepted, weren’t chosen, weren’t wanted. She had known before what it means to be an outsider: a refugee stripped of citizenship, for years she was “superfluous” to states and societies. She wrote about the “conscious pariah” — a person who, not being accepted, does not try at any cost to become an insider, but keeps the freedom of their own view. It follows that rejection by one group or one person does not take away your ability to be your own companion and to appear among other people. “Who” you are, for Arendt, is not determined by whether you were accepted in a particular place.
rejection.practice: Spend five minutes alone with yourself in silence and ask: “What do I myself think of me right now?” This companion’s answer weighs more than someone else’s “no.”

abandonment.text: Arendt considered “not belonging to the world” the most painful experience a person can have — she wrote about it in The Origins of Totalitarianism. The fear of being abandoned is the fear of losing your support in other people, and it touches exactly this. That is why the fear of being left alone is so strong: it concerns not only a particular person but your sense of your place in the world. Arendt also has an idea about how people create support for one another: through promises and mutual faithfulness. She acknowledged that another person is free and unpredictable — that is the price we pay for living among free people. But promises create islands of reliability. In other words, the fear of abandonment is not cured by complete control over another. Support comes from many connections — and from the promises we give and receive.
abandonment.practice: Recall one promise someone made you and kept, and thank that person — in a message or aloud when you meet.

unrequited.text: How many times can you replay the same conversation in your head? Unrequited love wounds deeply, and people of every age have known this pain. Arendt wrote a book about Rahel Varnhagen — a Berlin salon hostess at the turn of the 19th century who lived through several painful love affairs, including a broken engagement. Arendt showed how Rahel retreated into introspection — endless self-analysis in which the world and other people disappear and only one’s own feelings remain. Arendt considered this a trap: when the soul closes in on itself, it loses the world. Rahel’s way, for Arendt, lay in returning to reality, to people, to her own history. Arendt would probably say that unrequited love easily turns into an endless conversation with yourself about the other person. The pain is legitimate. But the world is still here, and in it there are people ready to see you.
unrequited.practice: Do one thing today that brings you back into the world: a meeting, a walk, a conversation about something else. Notice what has changed.

humiliation.text: Arendt derived the formula “the right to have rights” from the fate of stateless people — her own included: human dignity is vulnerable when a person isn’t recognized as a member of the shared world. Humiliation strikes exactly there, as if you had been stripped of the right to be an equal. She emphasized that equality is not a given of nature but something people create among themselves when they recognize one another. Carrying Arendt’s thought further, humiliation speaks of a violation of this recognition, not of your worth. Arendt also said: if you are attacked for who you are, you must defend yourself as who you are. That means not agreeing with the humiliating image and keeping your “who” in your own eyes.
humiliation.practice: Stand up straight, feel the floor under your feet, and say aloud: “I was treated as if I were… But I am…”, finishing the second part with the truth about yourself.

body_shame.text: The pattern on a butterfly’s wing or a seashell, the biologist Adolf Portmann observed, often serves not survival but simply display — Arendt was delighted by this idea. If you’re unhappy with your body, it is often tied to how we look in other people’s eyes. In The Life of the Mind, Arendt wrote about “appearance”: everything alive has an urge to show itself, to appear — and this is not a flaw but the very nature of the living. The world is arranged like a stage on which every living thing appears in its own unique form. For Arendt, the body is your way of appearing to the world, and there is no “correct” shape for that. Moreover, “who” you are, for Arendt, is disclosed above all in words and deeds. The body is your presence in the world, not a scorecard.
body_shame.practice: Choose one action or word for today through which you will appear to the world not by your looks but as “who” you are — and do it.

illness.text: Intense bodily pain, Arendt wrote in The Human Condition, is the most intense feeling we know and at the same time the most private, almost incommunicable. When the body lets you down, illness makes life narrower and heavier. Pain seems to cut a person off from the shared world: it is hard to show, and others cannot feel it for you. Arendt suggests that illness threatens not only the body but also your connection with the world. That is why it matters so much that you keep the possibility of speaking and being heard. Arendt valued storytelling: by turning experience into a story, a person brings it back into the shared world. You don’t have to explain your pain fully, but you can share at least part of it — and so the illness becomes less lonely.
illness.practice: Tell one person how your day with the illness went — without complaining or embellishing, simply telling it. This, for Arendt, is how pain returns to the shared world.

pride.text: Homo faber, the maker, has every right to pride in Arendt’s account: he sees a thing leave his hands and enter the world, a thing that will outlast him. Pride in what you’ve done is a healthy feeling that needn’t be hidden. In The Human Condition she distinguished “labor,” “work” and “action.” “Work” is the making of things that outlast us and make the world stable: a table, a book, a house. Work has a beginning and an end, and its result can be shown to others. And in “action,” who you are is disclosed. It follows that healthy pride is the joy of having left something in the world that wasn’t there before. It is not superiority over others but participation in the shared world. Such a feeling can be shared — by showing people what you have made.
pride.practice: Show what you’re proud of to one person who might find it interesting — let what you’ve made appear in the shared world.

melancholy.text: Arendt’s friend, the philosopher Walter Benjamin, said he was born “under the sign of Saturn,” the planet of melancholy, and she wrote one of her tenderest essays about him. Gentle sadness is a quiet feeling in which sorrow and tenderness for the past are intertwined. Arendt compared Benjamin to a “pearl diver”: he dove into the depths of the past and brought up to the surface individual precious fragments so that they could shine again. In other words, melancholy can be not decline but a special form of attention — to what passes, to the beauty of what has been lost. It needs neither treatment nor banishing. Bright sadness lets you see the “pearls” of your past — and carry them into the present.
melancholy.practice: Write down in a few words one “pearl” — a small moment from the past that still glows — like an entry in the “thought diary” Arendt kept for over twenty years.
